newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Dec 13.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Dec 13.

text.p: THE DOMINION

NZ First MPs were considering on Thursday night whether to snub National after just a day in coalition, by supporting Labour's Jonathan Hunt for Deputy Speaker on Friday. The opening of the first MMP parliament was soured on Thursday by resentment on the opposition benches at the National-NZ First coalition plan to provide both the Speaker, Doug Kidd, and the Deputy Speaker from its own ranks. Kidd defeated Hunt 70 to 50 for the Speaker's job in the first contested election for the post in 73 years. United NZ MP Peter Dunne and ACT NZ's 8 MPs voted with the government. Page 1.

Singapore development company Pidemco Land has canned its first investment in New Zealand -- buying land at Lake Taupo for a $32 million hotel and resort -- citing a Maori land claim as a significant problem. Pidemco had signed a purchase agreement with Landcorp for 241 hectares of land in Wellington two years ago. But Pidemco, government-owned and one of Singapore's biggest property comapnies with interests in China and Vietnam, said on Thursday the sale would not go ahead. Page 1.

The government is understood to have offered National list MP Jim Gerard a plum post as New Zealand's high commissioner to Canada as compensation for sidelining him in the search for a new Speaker. Gerard is understood to be considering the offer. He dismissed speculation that he would resign, saying: "I'm not in a huff and I'm not resigning." However, he would not comment on whether he would still be a National MP in a year's time. Page 1.

Backbench National MPs have given a guarded thumbs-up to their party's coalition agreement with NZ First, though concerns remain at the deferral of tax cuts and the number of cabinet posts offered to NZ First. MPs spoken to indicated many aspects of the coalition deal, such as extra social spending and changes to the health system, would have been considered by a National government anyway. Page 2.

ACT NZ has refused to fully sanction the National and NZ First policy package, leaving the fledging coalition government vulnerable to floor-crossing by government MPs. ACT leader Richard Prebble said he was concerned that National's big consessions on social spending would send the economy into a tailspin. Page 2.

NZ First has lost support since the October 12 general election, according to a TV One-Colmar Brunton poll broadcast on Thursday night. It shows NZ First down to eight percent support from the 13 percent it gained on election night. National gained one point to 35 percent, Labour stayed the same on 28 percent, the Alliance went down to seven percent from 10 percent and ACT NZ dropped to 4.5 percent from six percent. Page 2.

About 350,000 AMP policyholders in New Zealand might be in for a windfall of shares if the insurance group's members around the world agree to give up "mutual" status and list on the Stock Exchange. AMP New Zealand general manager Rodney Cook said on Thursday that the longer a policy had been held and the bigger it was, the greater the potential value of the share giveaway. There would be an unspecified minimum parccel of shares for any policyholder which would be "very attractive", he said. Members would probably vote on the proposal towards the end of 1997. Page 14.

Clear Communications claimed victory on Thursday over rival Telecom after the announcement of National-NZ First's telecommunications policy, but Telecom cast doubt on the policy's significance and meaning. While Clear spokeswoman Janiene Bayliss hailed the policy as "a new era for the telecommunications industry", Telecom spokesman Clive Litt said the government would be approached for clarification. The agreement's telecommunictions policy says the preference is for the Commerce Commission and the Commerce Ministry to address competition issues. On the issues of "media domination" and "cross media ownership", the agreement says the situation will be kept under review. Page 14.

The export credit guarantee scheme proposed by the coalition government is seen as a positive step that should greatly benefit exporters. The scheme should provide medium- and long-term insurance cover for exporters sold into higher-risk areas, insurers said on Thursday. The coalition government has proposed a scheme that would offer a guarantee line of up to $50 million a year for three years. This would provide insurance against non-payment for exports. Page 14.
Public consultation has taken a heavy toll on Lambton Harbour Management's finances, with the company reporting a $4.22 million drop in tax-paid profit to $742,000 for the year to June 30. Page 14.
THE NEW ZEALAND HERALD

The Prime Minister has offered the position of High Commissioner to Canada to the National list MP Jim Gerard as a sop for his not becoming Speaker. The post is now held by a former National cabinet minister, Maurice McTigue, but his three-year term ends in April. Gerard is understood to be considering the offer. If he accepts, his place as an MP will be taken by Annabel Young, the next person on National's list. Labour Minister Doug Kidd on Thursday became the first Speaker of the MMP era after beating off a challenge from Labour's Jonathan Hunt by 70 votes to 50.

The Prime Minster faces the agonising task of having to dump at least two cabinet ministers, thanks to the concessions in the coalition deal with NZ First. With the coalition document signed and the Speaker elected, Jim Bolger may unveil the new line-up of ministers on Sunday. With fewer seats to allocate and the need to freshen his team Bolger is likely to sacrifice the Lands Minister Denis Marshall and Social Welfare Minister Peter Gresham, to being in two high-profile backbenchers, Max Bradford and Christine Fletcher.

The likely employment minister, Peter McCardle, has defended the new government's work-for-dole scheme as more compassionate than the "workfare" schemes tried overseas. At least two big city mayors have welcomed the prospect of putting unemployed labour to work on their projects. On Thursday, unemployed activists slated the plan, which will force those on the dole to work or train for up to two days a week in return for the money. They compared it to periodic detention.

At least half of the 480 staff at regional health authorities are expected to lose their jobs in the next 16 months. Health authority bosses have called a meeting in Wellington with caretaker Health Minister Jenny Shipley and key ministry staff, to learn more about the latest round of restructuring.

About 350,000 New Zealand policyholders of the AMP Society can look forward to a windfall in late 1998, if it opts to demutualise next year. AMP has been deliberating for a year on whether to follow National Mutual and Colonial Mutual in converting from a mutual society, owned by its 2.3 million policyholders, to a company with shareholders. Its directors this week voted to recommend demutualisation. Details of the proposal will be put to members on the middle of next year ahead of the vote.

Sharemarket analysts on Thursday concluded that the capital reduction announced by brewer DB Group this week was a good deal for shareholders. The company was overcapitalised and the proposed cancellation of three out of every four shares and a payment of 60 cents a share would reduce the company's cost of capital because equity was far more expensive than debt, they said. DB chairman David Sadler estimated that the shares remaining after cancellation would be worth about 200 cents. But this was seen as too low by analysts. Cavill White Securities' John Cairns said the shares could be worth up to 270 cents based on a predicted September 1997 year profit of $20 million.

Dunedin-based Wilson Neill, which faces winding-up action, has had nearly all its shareholders' funds wiped out by a $2.46 million loss in the September year. With equity now of just $4,000 -- $2.3 million 12 months ago -- and 337 million shares on issue, the net tangible asset backing of Wilson Neill is effectively nil.

Weakness on global bond markets and domestic uncertainty over next week's Reserve Bank monetary policy statement produced a lukewarm response to Thursday's tender of $100 million of February 2001 government stock. The tender attracted a meagre $167 million in bids, well below the $404 million bid for $100 million of the same stock on October 31.
-- Wellington newsroom (64 4) 473 4746
